passage.title: Nine Billion Ticks Per Second
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Bank
passage.text:
For centuries, people kept time by watching a brass weight swing or a quartz crystal hum inside a watch. Yet even the finest quartz watch drifts off by a tiny fraction of a second each day. For someone walking to school, losing a thousandth of a second does not matter at all. For a fleet of space probes guiding planes and phones on Earth, though, that small drift would be a wreck. To pinpoint a spot on the globe within a few feet, space clocks must never waver.

Each Global Positioning System craft circles Earth twelve thousand miles up in the dark sky. From that high path, it sends down a steady stream of radio time stamps. Your phone compares the exact instant a signal left the craft with the moment it reached the ground. Because radio waves move at the speed of light, they cross roughly one foot in a single billionth of a second. If a space clock drifted by just one thousandth of a second, your map pin would miss your street by nearly two hundred miles.

To stop such huge errors, scientists built atomic clocks around a soft gray metal called cesium. Every atom of this metal has a single outer charge that spins like a tiny magnet around the core. When a beam of waves strikes the atom at the exact right pitch, that outer charge flips its spin state. Unlike a brass rod that swells in summer heat, every cesium atom in the cosmos flips at the exact same rate.

Inside the vacuum tube of an atomic clock, pure metal is warmed until a stream of gas atoms drifts down a pipe. Inside the shielded chamber of the clock, the drifting cesium atoms are struck by a tuned wave beam before they reach the far sensor. When the wave pitch hits precisely 9,192,631,770 cycles per second, the most atoms flip state and light up the sensor. A smart loop locks the crystal timer to that exact count. That steady beat defines the true length of one second.

High in space, four atomic clocks ride aboard each GPS craft so the fleet always has a spare. Ground crews also tune those space clocks for subtle time shifts caused by high speed and weak pull in orbit. Thanks to nine billion steady ticks per second, hikers, pilots, and rescue teams can find their way anywhere on Earth.

tier2Words.definition: To locate or identify something with extreme accuracy
tier2Words.rootHint: Compound of 'pin' + 'point' — finding a spot as small as the tip of a pin
tier2Words.contextClue: Space clocks must be accurate to locate a spot on the globe within just a few feet.

tier2Words.definition: A sealed space from which air and other gases have been pumped out
tier2Words.contextClue: Inside the empty, air-free tube of the clock, gas atoms drift without bumping into air.

tier2Words.definition: Exactly and sharply, with zero error or guesswork
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'praecisus' meaning cut off cleanly or exact
tier2Words.contextClue: The wave beam must hit the exact number of 9,192,631,770 cycles per second.

tier2Words.definition: Very slight, delicate, or hard to notice without sensitive tools
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'subtilis' meaning fine or delicate
tier2Words.contextClue: Ground crews tune the clocks for tiny time shifts caused by high speed and weak pull in orbit.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Inside the shielded chamber of the clock, the drifting cesium atoms are struck by a tuned wave beam before they reach the far sensor."

In this sentence, what performs the action of striking the cesium atoms?

options.text: The drifting cesium atoms inside the chamber
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice flips the action! The drifting cesium atoms receive the strike in Paragraph 4 instead of doing the striking.

options.text: A tuned wave beam inside the clock
options.childFeedback: Spot on! In Paragraph 4, the words 'by a tuned wave beam' right after 'are struck' show that the wave beam strikes the cesium atoms.

options.text: The far sensor at the end of the vacuum tube
options.childFeedback: Watch out—'before they reach the far sensor' tells where the atoms are heading in Paragraph 4, not what strikes them.

options.text: A brass weight swinging inside the space craft
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 3 mentions brass pendulums in old wall clocks on Earth, not inside space clocks.

questions.provingSentenceText: Inside the shielded chamber of the clock, the drifting cesium atoms are struck by a tuned wave beam before they reach the far sensor.
questions.childTip: Spot on! In Paragraph 4, the words 'by a tuned wave beam' right after 'are struck' show that the wave beam strikes the cesium atoms.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive construction, 'the drifting cesium atoms' receives the action ('are struck'). The agent phrase 'by a tuned wave beam' names what performs the action.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 4, find the action phrase 'are struck' and look right after 'by' to see what hits the cesium atoms.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 1:

"To pinpoint a spot on the globe within a few feet, space clocks must never waver."

What does the word "pinpoint" most nearly mean as used in this sentence?

options.text: Fasten with a sharp metal needle
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice takes the word part 'pin' too literally; space satellites use radio signals, not metal needles.

options.text: Broadcast a loud warning to
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 1 explains that GPS clocks help a phone map a user's location on a street, not broadcast warnings.

options.text: Miss by nearly two hundred miles
options.childFeedback: Careful—missing by two hundred miles is the error described in Paragraph 2 when a clock is off, which is the opposite of pinpointing a spot.

options.text: Find the exact location of
options.childFeedback: Spot on! In Paragraph 1, 'pinpoint a spot on the globe within a few feet' means to find the exact location of a place with high accuracy.

questions.provingSentenceText: To pinpoint a spot on the globe within a few feet, space clocks must never waver.
questions.childTip: Spot on! In Paragraph 1, 'pinpoint a spot on the globe within a few feet' means to find the exact location of a place with high accuracy.
questions.parentExplanation: In context, 'pinpoint a spot on the globe within a few feet' means to locate or determine a position with extreme precision.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 1, notice the clue 'within a few feet'—space clocks must locate a spot on Earth with extreme accuracy.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 2, why does a tiny clock error of just one thousandth of a second cause a massive map error on the ground?

options.text: Radio waves move at the speed of light, covering roughly one foot every billionth of a second.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraph 2 explains that because radio waves travel at the speed of light—about one foot every billionth of a second—even a tiny timing error adds up to nearly two hundred miles.

options.text: Clouds and rain slow the radio time stamps down as they pass through the lower sky.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 2 never blames clouds or rain; the huge distance error comes from how fast light and radio waves travel.

options.text: Space craft stop sending signals whenever a phone user walks down a narrow street.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 1 states that space clocks help a phone locate a user on a narrow street, not that satellites stop sending signals there.

options.text: Phones must bounce their signals off the moon before comparing time stamps.
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraph 1 states that GPS signals travel straight from satellites twelve thousand miles up to your phone, never bouncing off the moon.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because radio waves move at the speed of light, they cross roughly one foot in a single billionth of a second.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraph 2 explains that because radio waves travel at the speed of light—about one foot every billionth of a second—even a tiny timing error adds up to nearly two hundred miles.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 explains the cause-and-effect link: because radio signals move at the speed of light (about one foot per nanosecond), even a one-millisecond timing error translates into nearly two hundred miles of distance error.
questions.retryHint: Look in Paragraph 2 for the sentence that explains how fast radio waves move in a billionth of a second.

questions.prompt: Why does the author contrast a cesium atom with "a brass rod that swells in summer heat" in Paragraph 3?

options.text: To argue that brass rods work better than cesium clocks during cold winter months
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraph 3 explains that brass rods change length with temperature and lose time, making them much less reliable than cesium clocks.

options.text: To show that every cesium atom flips at an unchanging rate regardless of outside conditions
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraph 3 contrasts a heat-sensitive brass rod with cesium atoms to show that every cesium atom in the universe flips at the exact same unchanging rate.

options.text: To explain why space craft must carry heavy brass rods alongside their four atomic clocks
options.childFeedback: Watch out—GPS satellites carry atomic clocks in Paragraph 5, not old-fashioned brass pendulum rods.

options.text: To prove that summer heat melts the soft gray metal inside watch batteries
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 4 mentions gentle heating inside the clock chamber to turn cesium into gas, not summer heat melting watch batteries.

questions.provingSentenceText: Unlike a brass rod that swells in summer heat, every cesium atom in the cosmos flips at the exact same rate.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraph 3 contrasts a heat-sensitive brass rod with cesium atoms to show that every cesium atom in the universe flips at the exact same unchanging rate.
questions.parentExplanation: Mechanical rods change length with temperature and thus change speed, whereas every cesium atom in the cosmos transitions at an identical, invariant rate.
questions.retryHint: Look at the last sentence of Paragraph 3 to see how cesium atoms differ from a brass rod.

questions.prompt: Part A: How does an atomic clock know when its wave beam is tuned to the exact right pitch?

options.text: The outer charges stop spinning completely and fall into the center of the atom.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 4 explains that the wave beam makes the outer charges flip their spin state, not stop spinning or fall into the core.

options.text: The gray cesium gas freezes into a solid crystal block inside the vacuum tube.
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraph 4 says a heater warms soft cesium metal into a faint gas stream, never freezing it into a block.

options.text: A ground crew sends a laser flash twelve thousand miles up to reset the chamber.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 4 explains that the clock's own detector counts the flipped atoms and locks the wave beam on target automatically.

options.text: The greatest number of cesium atoms flip their spin state and light up the sensor.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraph 4 explains that when the wave pitch hits exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles per second, the greatest number of cesium atoms flip state and light up the sensor.

questions.provingSentenceText: When the wave pitch hits precisely 9,192,631,770 cycles per second, the most atoms flip state and light up the sensor.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraph 4 explains that when the wave pitch hits exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles per second, the greatest number of cesium atoms flip state and light up the sensor.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explains that when the wave pitch matches 9,192,631,770 cycles per second, the maximum number of cesium atoms flip state and light up the sensor.
questions.retryHint: Check Paragraph 4 to see what happens at the sensor when the wave beam hits 9,192,631,770 cycles per second.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Yet even the finest quartz watch drifts off by a tiny fraction of a second each day."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this line from Paragraph 2 only explains why ordinary quartz wristwatches are not accurate enough for GPS.

options.text: "Every atom of this metal has a single outer charge that spins like a tiny magnet around the core."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this detail from Paragraph 3 describes the structure of a cesium atom, not how the sensor detects the right wave pitch.

options.text: "When the wave pitch hits precisely 9,192,631,770 cycles per second, the most atoms flip state and light up the sensor."
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This quote from Paragraph 4 directly proves Question 5 by showing that the sensor lights up with the most flipped atoms at 9,192,631,770 cycles per second.

options.text: "High in space, four atomic clocks ride aboard each GPS craft so the fleet always has a spare."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this sentence from Paragraph 5 only tells how many spare atomic clocks ride aboard each GPS satellite.

questions.provingSentenceText: When the wave pitch hits precisely 9,192,631,770 cycles per second, the most atoms flip state and light up the sensor.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This quote from Paragraph 4 directly proves Question 5 by showing that the sensor lights up with the most flipped atoms at 9,192,631,770 cycles per second.
